subject: Climate & Environment
title: Can We Stop the Sixth Extinction
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Can We Stop the Sixth Extinction.

hook.text: The sixth mass extinction is not inevitable. It is a choice we are making every day.

buildup.text: Conservation works — species recover when given protection, space, and time.

discovery.text: Bald eagles, wolves, whales, and pandas all prove that decline can be reversed.

twist.text: But recovery takes decades. Extinction takes a moment. We must act faster than we destroy.

climax.text: Protecting 30% of Earth, ending overfishing, and restoring habitats would bend the curve.

punchline.text: We are the first species that can choose to stop an extinction.

quiz.question: What proves that species decline can be reversed?
options: Success stories like eagles, whales, and pandas

details.summary: Stopping the sixth extinction requires protecting 30 to 50 percent of land and ocean, transforming agriculture, eliminating pollution, fighting climate change, and curbing wildlife trade. Progress is happening but not fast enough; current commitments fall far short of what science demands.
details.whyItMatters: The question is no longer whether a crisis exists but whether humanity will act at the speed and scale required. Every year of delay makes recovery harder and costlier.
takeaways: Habitat protection must at least double in the next decade
Agriculture needs to produce more food on less land with fewer chemicals
International cooperation and funding remain the biggest bottlenecks

faq.question: What is the single most important action to stop extinction?
faq.answer: Protecting and restoring natural habitat has the greatest impact because habitat loss is the leading extinction driver. Everything else, including pollution control and climate action, amplifies the benefit but cannot substitute for physical space for nature.

faq.question: How much would it cost to solve the biodiversity crisis?
faq.answer: Estimates range from 150 to 500 billion dollars per year, depending on scope. Current global biodiversity spending is roughly 100 billion. The funding gap is large but small compared to fossil fuel subsidies of over 500 billion annually.
